newsitem.title: USA: New try seen to end Pentagon payments for mergers.
newsitem.headline: New try seen to end Pentagon payments for mergers.

text.p: Conservative Republican Rep. Chris Smith said Tuesday he would join again in an unusual coalition with liberals to work against what he called "corporate welfare" that offers "payoffs for lay-offs."
Smith said he would introduce the "Pay-offs for Layoffs Corporate Welfare Elimination Act of 1997" in the last week of February.

At issue is the Pentagon practice of rewarding defense contractors for coming up with economies that are passed on to the government in the form of lower costs for military projects. The Pentagon says it rewards such economies, sometimes obtained through lay-offs, by reimbursing up to half the savings achieved.
Smith, of New Jersey, and independent Bernie Sanders of Vermont want to end the practice.

Those now in line for such possible reimbursements include Boeing in its merger with McDonnell Douglas and Raytheon in its proposed acquisitions of Texas Instruments and of General Motors Corp's Hughes Aircraft.

Last year the House passed a Smith-Sanders bill that would have eliminated the reimbursements. It never became law but Congress settled on softer compromise language limiting reimbursements to half of all savings, far short of what Smith and Sanders were trying to achieve.

"Uncle Sam is subsidizing big corporate mergers and acquisitions, which by design are intended to throw thousands of people out of work," Smith said last June in arguing for the bill. His views have not changed.
Smith is especially sensitive about the matter because 3,200 jobs were lost in his district when Lockheed merged with Martin Marietta to become Lockheed Martin.
"We are subsidizing and facilitating the loss of those jobs," Smith said in a CBS TV broadcast on Dec. 29.
Sanders is equally vociferous, and Tuesday said the government was providing "financial incentives to defense contractors so that they can lay off American workers."
Pentagon officials see the practice quite differently.

"What we're trying to do is provide some incentives for our industry to be more efficient," Paul Kaminski, the under secretary of defense for acquisition and technology, told reporters late last month.

He said when two companies merge they can often save money by "reducing unnecessary overhead staff." The government pegs its payments to companies in part to their overhead costs, so when overhead costs go down it saves money.
